generalfeedback.text:
One valid proof (taking the two sub-intervals in the order \([a,b]\) then \([b,c]\) — the reverse order works just as well):

Since \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(f(a)=f(b)=0\), Rolle's Theorem gives a point \(p\in(a,b)\) with \(f'(p)=0\).

Since \(f\) is continuous on \([b,c]\), differentiable on \((b,c)\), and \(f(b)=f(c)=0\), Rolle's Theorem gives a point \(q\in(b,c)\) with \(f'(q)=0\). Here \(p

Now \(f'\) is continuous on \([p,q]\) and differentiable on \((p,q)\) (since \(f\) is twice differentiable), and \(f'(p)=f'(q)=0\). Rolle's Theorem applied to \(f'\) on \([p,q]\) gives an element \(r\in(p,q)\) with \((f')'(r)=f''(r)=0\), as required.
